title: A shop worth keeping
speaker: tenant_salmah
dialogue: My parents taught me to repair things other people would throw away. Now the rent keeps going up, and visitors take photos of the shop more often than they bring things to repair. Like that, how to convince an apprentice there is a future here?
question: Protect the lease, fund an apprentice, or invest in shared ownership?
options: Keep independent traders in place, with owner compensation.
Pay for skills to be taught; rent pressure remains.
Put premises into shared ownership at a high upfront cost.
consequence: Rent relief buys time. Apprenticeships preserve practice. Shared ownership needs capacity that could fund other needs.

title: Who learns the next verse?
speaker: custodian_rahim
dialogue: At Kreta Ayer Heritage Gallery, we have records of opera, puppetry and all these practices. But in our imagined neighbourhood workshop, we still need people to teach and learn. Put a costume on display, can. But that cannot replace years of practice, right? Who will have the time and space to learn?
question: Support teaching, secure a home for it, or adapt another space?
options: Fund mentoring and time to practise.
Bring an old unit into use while retaining its archive.
consequence: An archive protects records, while active teaching sustains continuity. More commercial demand can still displace learners.

title: The missing teacher
speaker: custodian_rahim
dialogue: The recordings are there. But now nobody here remembers how to correct the little mistakes. The teaching chain is broken already. We can start again with what is left, but cannot say everything is recovered just like that.
question: Rebuild teaching, secure long-term space, or protect surviving records?
options: Rebuild practice gradually; lost knowledge limits recovery.
Secure space for a long commitment.
Keep surviving records inside a newly used space.
consequence: Once continuity crosses the lasting-loss threshold, grants cannot instantly restore it.

title: Room around a living temple
speaker: youth_faiz
dialogue: Around Thian Hock Keng, people come to pray, work and visit. Busy is good, but the neighbours must be comfortable also. Can some visitor spending support shared spaces and affordable shops nearby? And we must respect the temple, of course.
question: Share visitor income, support nearby community premises, or invest in learning?
options: Support community ownership of nearby premises.
Raise funds and distribute benefits, with a ten-year sunset.
Make learning and participation more viable.
consequence: A busy district does not automatically share its gains. Equity needs direct support.

title: The walk between stops
speaker: operator_jo
dialogue: On the brochure, the route looks fine. But in the afternoon, so hot. People need shade and somewhere to rest. Our staff and suppliers use these streets also, you know. The route must work for everyday life, not just the tours.
question: Cool buildings, shade the route, or raise capacity first?
options: Add shade and walking space while retaining a loading window.
Fund community improvements, with a sunset review.
consequence: Cooling directly improves habitability. Pedestrianisation also attracts activity and can increase rent pressure.

title: A crowd is not a community
speaker: operator_jo
dialogue: A busy street helps my staff earn a living. But if every shop chases the same tourists, the regular customers come back for what? I want the visitor business to do well, lah, but leave some room for everyday neighbourhood life also.
question: Redistribute benefits, protect traders, or expand evening activity?
options: Share visitor income, accepting some loss of demand.
Protect existing traders from rising rent pressure.
Bring more evening activity, with a quiet-hours agreement.
consequence: High vitality alongside weak continuity can lock the district into visitor monoculture.

title: More than a preserved doorway
speaker: custodian_rahim
dialogue: The Chinatown Heritage Centre remembers how the early migrants lived. But the shophouses nearby need a future also. When a new business takes over, will it keep space for local stories and skills? Or just put up some heritage decorations and call it a day?
question: Adapt the space, support teaching, or pursue shared ownership?
options: Allow new activity with an archive protection clause.
Fund living practice instead of a display alone.
consequence: Reuse brings activity but may increase rent pressure. Records alone do not keep a living practice alive.

title: More than the lunch queue
speaker: tenant_salmah
dialogue: At Maxwell Food Centre, people come together over a meal. In this imagined future, the hawkers want more evening business. Understandable, lah, but their day already starts so early. Can we help them earn a living and keep access comfortable, without making life harder for the neighbours?
question: Extend evenings, improve comfort, or make room for walking?
options: Expand evening activity with a noise curfew.
Improve walking and shade with delivery access.
consequence: A curfew reduces some harms; it does not remove the long-term trade-offs of night activity.

title: A table for the neighbourhood
speaker: youth_faiz
dialogue: At Chinatown Complex, you come for a meal and see familiar faces also. But in this imagined future, older neighbours and young workers are finding it harder to afford life here. Can visitor income help them? Or should we put the money into community space and the next generation of hawkers?
question: Share visitor income, support community premises, or fund the next generation?
options: Support community ownership of nearby premises.
Raise funds and distribute benefits, with a ten-year sunset.
Make learning and participation more viable.
consequence: A busy district does not automatically share its gains. Equity needs direct support.
